title: Arguments Proving From Antiquity the Dignity, Power, and Jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery (1616 royal decision)
citation: Royal judgment of July 18, 1616; 21 Eng. Rep. 576–598
lead: A conflict between the King’s courts prompted an inquiry into whether Chancery could restrain enforcement of a sound common-law judgment for reasons of equity; James I approved that established equitable jurisdiction.

actors.name: James I
actors.role: King resolving the jurisdictional conflict and ordering enrollment

actors.name: King’s Bench and Chancery
actors.role: Courts in conflict over postjudgment equitable relief

actors.name: The Chancellor
actors.role: Officer referring the hypothetical and directed to continue proper equitable relief

actors.name: Francis Bacon, Henry Montagu, Henry Yelverton, Randall Crew, and John Walter
A and B
actors.role: Hypothetical judgment creditor and debtor, not identified actual litigants

actors.name: Anonymous compiler
actors.role: Later author reproducing and defending the historical instruments

proceedings: Royal request for verified precedents; counsel’s first certificate; further referral of hypothetical and unanimous legal certificate; King’s July 18, 1616 ratification and direction to enroll the proceedings.
limits: This is a retrospective tract containing a royal jurisdictional instrument, not a conventional party-captioned appellate case. The compiler’s advocacy, counsel’s advice, and royal command have distinct authority. No debt recovery or judgment on actual A/B litigation was entered.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Conflicting views of Chancery’s power reached the King
sections.cue: Introduce the asserted statutory limits and source components.
paragraphs: King’s Bench and Chancery disputed whether equity could intervene after a common-law judgment. Opponents invoked the praemunire statute of 27 Edward III, chapter 1, and a prohibition under 4 Henry IV. The reproduced tract calls the latter chapter 23 in some discussion but chapter 22 when reproducing its text; the source contains that variation.

James I directed his Attorney General, assisted by learned counsel, to inspect original Chancery precedents and report. The later anonymous compilation, Arguments Proving From Antiquity the Dignity, Power, and Jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, reproduces the resulting certificates and royal decision amid historical advocacy. Its opening mentions Coke’s Institutes after Coke’s death, so the tract’s retrospective discussion is distinct from its embedded 1616 instrument.

sections.title: Counsel verified a continuing practice and examined a hypothetical
sections.cue: Keep the model parties separate from an actual case record.
paragraphs: Counsel’s first certificate returned thirteen observations supported by original records. The practice continued from Henry VII through the current Chancellor and covered real and personal actions, multiple common-law courts, verdicts, demurrers, and writs of error. Equity could follow judgment and even execution, often on grounds existing beforehand rather than a later bargain.

The Chancellor then referred a hypothetical. A had obtained judgment and execution against B for a £1,000 debt and ejectment involving the manor of D. B accepted that the judgments were correct under strict common-law rules but claimed equitable grounds unavailable through error, attaint, or other common-law remedies. No actual debtor biography, manor trial, or recovery was reported.

The Prince’s Attorney joined the advisers for the second inquiry. They examined statutes, parliamentary petitions and royal answers, and authorities on both sides. Francis Bacon, Henry Montagu, Henry Yelverton, Randall Crew, and John Walter all subscribed the conclusion that Chancery could relieve in the proposed circumstances and no cited statute prohibited it.

sections.title: Established practice and the purpose of praemunire supported jurisdiction
sections.cue: Explain counsel’s reasons as advice, not separate judicial holdings.
paragraphs: Counsel found orders and decrees releasing judgments, preventing or correcting possession obtained through them, handling mesne profits, and releasing costs. Litigants sometimes expressly argued that judgment foreclosed equity and lost that objection. Common-law judges themselves directed parties to Chancery or exercised equitable authority while sitting there during a Chancellor’s absence. Sustained practice by trained magistrates informed counsel’s statutory reading.

Their eight praemunire reasons emphasized that the statute targeted prejudice to royal jurisdiction through another authority, while Chancery was itself the King’s court. The statutory remedy contemplated appearance in Chancery, making it implausible that the same court supplied both offense and remedy. Severe exclusion from royal protection fit adherence to foreign jurisdiction rather than excess within a royal tribunal. Related statutes, historical references, original petitions, translated forms, and common-law processes pointed toward foreign, papally subordinate, or ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

The advisers found indictments but no established convictions for this kind of Chancery proceeding. The compiler separately explained that indictment did not establish guilt and obtaining a pardon did not necessarily admit the supposed offense. Those were evidentiary observations, not a rule making indictment legally irrelevant.

sections.title: Counsel distinguished equity against a party from reversal of a legal judgment
sections.cue: Set out the domestic-statute analysis and the research limit.
paragraphs: The Henry IV provision concerned domestic proceedings, but counsel gave six reasons not to apply it here. Chancery was absent from the enumerated extraordinary processes. A preceding petition had expressly sought limits on Chancery and other ordinary procedures, and the royal answer preserved necessary resort to them.

More fundamentally, equity did not reopen the same legal question: the equitable issue had never been adjudicated at common law. Error and attaint reversed judgments, while proper Chancery relief addressed the prevailing party’s conscience. No conviction on the asserted theory was established. Requiring anticipatory equity before knowing whether common law would provide relief could also leave a deserving party without an effective remedy.

Counsel acknowledged that Chancery clerks had supplied precedents but King’s Bench officers had not produced indictment precedents. They offered to examine more if directed. Their statement about absent contrary convictions therefore reflected that limited examination, not an exhaustive assertion beyond it.

sections.title: James approved equitable protection on meritorious complaints
sections.cue: Give the royal direction without inventing an appellate mandate.
paragraphs: On July 18, 1616, in his fourteenth regnal year, James ratified the practice account and legal opinion as applied to the referred case. He commanded the Chancellor or Keeper of the Great Seal to continue relief warranted by the merits and justice of complaints despite common-law proceedings, consistently with ancient continuing Chancery practice. He asserted authority to settle jurisdictional differences among his courts and ordered enrollment to reduce future disputes. Bacon and Yelverton appear beneath the concluding formula.

The command did not authorize retrial whenever a common-law loser disliked the result. Its premise was equitable conscience distinct from the legal issue already decided and merit in the specific equitable cause. There was no modern affirmance, remand, judicial vote count, or monetary award to the hypothetical B.

sections.title: The later compiler expanded the defense through historical illustrations
sections.cue: Conclude with the limits of the surrounding advocacy.
paragraphs: The remaining tract discussed ancient courts, seals, writs, chancellors, law and equity, parliamentary forms, differences between petitions and printed statutes, statutory wording, grievances, and later practice. Those arguments were the compiler’s further defense, not additional operative terms of the King’s judgment.

An illustrative bond showed why a valid £800 judgment might require equitable restraint when only £20 remained unpaid. The compiler also distinguished Throgmorton’s litigation through forfeitures and the Queen’s interest, and argued that excluding equity for fraud, trust breaches, or forfeitures would allow injuries beyond error or attaint’s reach. These were examples and analysis, not findings or remedies in an actual A-versus-B case.
